title: Master Class | Caro–Kann x2!! | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: d4, c6, e4 — another Caro-Kann.

d5, the pawns trade on d5, and the knight to c3 — an inaccuracy, not huge, but after it White is basically fighting for equality. The knight to c3 blocks the c2-pawn, and with a pawn on d4, that pawn in effect becomes isolated, since the knight blocks its only pawn defense. c4 is the Panov Attack, a legitimate line, but the more solid line I recommend to beginners is the bishop to d3 and then c3, to protect the pawn with another pawn.
Then White's knight can develop eventually via d2. The knight to c6.
The knight to f3.
The knight to f6, developing.
The bishop to b5, the bishop to g4 — this is where you should ask questions if you have them.
And the queen to d3 is a good move. Now, if White had played h3, here's an instructive question —
— should we take on f3, or drop the bishop back to h5?
Let's see what people think.

The reason the bishop to d3 is good: if c3 immediately, you allow the bishop to come to f5, prime real estate on Broadway — you don't want to let that bishop develop there, so you play the bishop to d3 first.
Most people say drop it back, but I kind of tricked you — I think you should take.
As I said earlier, the rule for deciding when to take and when to procrastinate —
— is to procrastinate until the point of no return, the point at which your opponent can actually permanently prevent you from doing what you want to do.
And if you drop the bishop back —
— then why does the move g4, attacking the bishop, matter? Everybody should understand this.
The bishop to g6 — and guess what, you've lost the possibility of taking the knight. Why is that a problem?
The knight to e5 — a very unpleasant move. The whole point was to pin the knight and eventually take it, but now the knight jumps to e5; this isn't winning for White, but it's just very unpleasant.
You have to play the rook to c8, and then maybe h4 and h5 comes, and this bishop becomes the instrument of Black's demise — when it was supposed to be the instrument of White's.
You were supposed to use this bishop to take White's knight; now this bishop might get trapped.

Some people don't see this because you've been conditioned to think g4 is very weakening and something to induce — but stay away from categorical thoughts; g4 is far more weakening once White has castled, and even then there are many situations where it's perfectly justified. It's not as weakening as some make it out to be.
So be really careful — sometimes it's good to induce this move, but make sure you're not giving your opponent a big initiative. We actually would want to take this knight —

— and play as we did in the game: e6, the bishop to d6, castle, and maybe eventually the queen to b6 to increase pressure on the pawn. The queen to d3, we take, that's why we played e6, and the knight takes d5 gave up the game immediately. Taking on g4 is fine in plenty of positions, but generally when White has castled, be careful. As for what White should do here — I'd consider castling long, though it's very dangerous, since the d-pawn is weak and there's the semi-open c-file; castling short is bad because you blunder the pawn.
